name: Tikkun Olam
one_line_summary: Jewish concept of repairing the world through human action.
extended_summary: Tikkun Olam (Hebrew: 'repair of the world,' 'mending of the world,' 'perfecting of the world') is the Jewish concept that humans participate in the work of healing and perfecting the world. The phrase has substantially different meanings across Jewish history. In rabbinic literature (Mishnah Gittin 4, etc.), tikkun olam designated specific legal-rabbinical adjustments designed to maintain social order and prevent injustice — narrower and more technical than contemporary usage. In Lurianic Kabbalah (Isaac Luria, 16th century Safed), tikkun olam acquired its cosmic-theological meaning: the divine work of reassembling the divine sparks (nitzotzot) scattered through the broken vessels (shevirat ha-kelim) of an earlier creation, a work in which humans participate through prayer, mitzvot (commandments), and contemplative practice. The Aleinu prayer (recited at the end of every Jewish service) includes the phrase l'takken olam b'malkhut Shaddai ('to perfect the world under the sovereignty of God'), connecting tikkun olam to Jewish liturgical and eschatological hope. Contemporary American Jewish usage (substantially developed from the late 20th century onward, particularly within Reform and Conservative Judaism but increasingly across denominational lines) has expanded tikkun olam to designate Jewish commitment to social justice and progressive political engagement — though contemporary scholars including Jonathan Krasner and Lawrence Fine have argued this contemporary usage is somewhat detached from both the rabbinic and Lurianic meanings. The framework remains central to contemporary Jewish ethical and political thought.
originators: Mishnaic rabbinic tradition (technical legal sense); Aleinu prayer; Isaac Luria and Lurianic Kabbalah (cosmic-theological sense, 16th century Safed); contemporary American Jewish movements (social-justice expansion, late 20th century onward)
year_or_decade: Mishnaic period 1st-3rd century CE (rabbinic sense); 16th century (Lurianic cosmic sense); late 20th century (contemporary social-justice expansion)
core_components: Three principal historical meanings: rabbinic legal-technical (Mishnah); cosmic-theological (Lurianic Kabbalah, repair of broken vessels); contemporary social-justice (late 20th century onward); Connection to Aleinu prayer (l'takken olam); Connection to Lurianic doctrine of shevirat ha-kelim; Connection to mitzvot (commandments) and human-divine partnership; Foundation for Jewish ethical and political engagement; Substantial variation in contemporary usage; Tension between traditional and contemporary meanings
primary_use_case: Foundational concept in contemporary Jewish ethics and social-justice work; reference framework across Reform, Conservative, Reconstructionist, and increasingly other Jewish denominations; foundation for substantial Jewish nonprofit and advocacy work (American Jewish World Service, Jewish Funds for Justice, T'ruah, others); basis for Jewish engagement with environmental, racial-justice, immigration, and other social-justice causes; foundation for some Jewish liturgical and educational practices; growing influence in interfaith social-justice work.
common_criticisms: Contemporary social-justice usage has been argued by some scholars (Jonathan Krasner, Lawrence Fine) to be detached from both traditional rabbinic and Lurianic meanings — the contemporary 'tikkun olam means social justice' framing has limited textual support before the late 20th century; intra-Jewish debates about whether tikkun olam adequately captures Jewish ethical and political tradition or whether it has become buzzword obscuring more specific Jewish concepts; political usage spans liberal-progressive (more common American Jewish usage) and other framings, with disputes about whether tikkun olam can be neutral political vocabulary; tension between cosmic-theological framing (which presupposes Lurianic metaphysics) and contemporary uses that don't engage that theological foundation; concerns within Jewish community about appropriation outside Jewish religious context; cross-denominational variation in usage; Orthodox engagement with the term has been complicated, with some Orthodox figures embracing tikkun olam in social-justice senses and others objecting to what they see as ahistorical use.
primary_sources: Mishnah Gittin 4 (rabbinic legal sense); Aleinu prayer; Vital, C. (compiled, 16th-17th century). Etz Chayim (Lurianic teachings); Krasner, J.B. (2014). 'The Place of Tikkun Olam in American Jewish Life'; Fine, L. (2003). Physician of the Soul, Healer of the Cosmos

name: Beatitudes
one_line_summary: Christ's teachings in the Sermon on the Mount inverting conventional value hierarchies.
extended_summary: The Beatitudes (Latin: beatitudo = blessedness, happiness; Greek: makarismoi) are the eight (or nine in some readings) blessings with which Jesus opens the Sermon on the Mount in Matthew 5:3-12, with a parallel four-blessing version in Luke 6:20-26 (the Sermon on the Plain). The Matthean version: Blessed are the poor in spirit (theirs is the kingdom of heaven); the meek (they will inherit the earth); those who mourn (they will be comforted); those who hunger and thirst for righteousness (they will be filled); the merciful (they will receive mercy); the pure in heart (they will see God); the peacemakers (they will be called children of God); those persecuted for righteousness' sake (theirs is the kingdom of heaven); with a final blessing for those persecuted on Jesus's account. The Lucan version, more compact and with corresponding 'woes,' focuses on actual material poverty rather than 'poor in spirit.' The Beatitudes function as the foundational ethical and spiritual orientation of Christian discipleship, presenting an inverted value structure in which the apparent losers in worldly terms (the poor, mourning, persecuted) are revealed to be blessed in God's economy. Christian tradition has variously interpreted the Beatitudes: as ethical demands (what disciples must become); as eschatological promises (states that will be reversed in God's kingdom); as descriptions of Christ himself; or as stages in spiritual development. The Beatitudes have substantial influence on Christian ethics, social teaching (Catholic social doctrine, liberation theology), nonviolent resistance traditions (Gandhi, MLK), and interfaith dialogue.
originators: Foundational scripture: Sermon on the Mount in Matthew (Matthew 5:3-12) and Sermon on the Plain in Luke (Luke 6:20-26); subsequent Christian interpretive tradition
year_or_decade: 1st century CE (Gospel composition: Matthew ~80-90 CE, Luke ~80-90 CE); ongoing interpretive tradition
core_components: Eight (or nine) Matthean blessings; Four Lucan blessings with corresponding woes; Each blessing follows pattern: 'Blessed are X, for they shall Y'; Eschatological structure (present-future reversal); Various interpretive frameworks (ethical demands, eschatological promises, Christological description, spiritual stages); Connection to broader Sermon on the Mount; Foundation for Christian ethics and social teaching; Influence on nonviolent resistance traditions; Reception in Catholic social doctrine, liberation theology, Anabaptist and peace-church traditions
primary_use_case: Foundational scripture in Christian ethics and discipleship; reference framework in Christian moral theology; basis for substantial Christian preaching and spiritual formation; foundation for Christian engagement with poverty, peacemaking, and social justice; influence on Catholic social teaching and liberation theology; foundation for nonviolent resistance traditions (Gandhi explicitly drew on the Sermon on the Mount; MLK's theology incorporated the Beatitudes substantially); pedagogical framework in Christian education across denominations.
common_criticisms: Substantial interpretive disagreement about whether the Beatitudes describe states required of disciples (ethical demand reading), states blessed by God independent of disciples' choices (eschatological promise reading), Christ himself (Christological reading), or stages of spiritual development — these differ substantially in implication; the spiritualized Matthean 'poor in spirit' has been argued (notably by Latin American liberation theology) to soften the more direct Lucan 'poor' in ways that domesticate the radical economic implications; tension between eschatological reversal framing (the kingdom is coming, present orders will be overturned) and ethical-prescription framing (we should be merciful now); cross-translation issues with 'blessed' (makarios) — variants include 'happy,' 'fortunate,' or 'congratulated' that shift connotation; some interpretive traditions have argued the Beatitudes apply only to the future kingdom rather than current discipleship, undercutting their ethical force; cross-cultural application of Mediterranean-Christian framings; tension between the Beatitudes' radical implications and historical Christian institutional practice that has often departed from them; popular sentimental reception sometimes empties the radical content of specific blessings (especially those addressing persecution and poverty).
primary_sources: Gospel of Matthew 5:3-12 (Sermon on the Mount); Gospel of Luke 6:20-26 (Sermon on the Plain); Augustine. Sermon on the Mount (early 5th century); Aquinas, T. Summa Theologiae I-II Q.69 on the Beatitudes; Bonhoeffer, D. (1937). The Cost of Discipleship
siblings: Theological Virtues; Seven Deadly Sins; Cardinal Virtues
